scribe_response.text: Tell me about a time you moved to a new place. The biggest move in my life was a long time ago, in the spring. Alan had been, been gone for um two years, and the house in Headingley had um grown far too quiet. Helen rang me every Sunday from Abu Dhabi, and every Sunday she asked the same question. She asked if I would come and live near her and the little ones. I said no for a long time, because we stay put up north. Then one morning I fell on the ice outside, and that made me decide. I was not hurt, but I lay, lay there looking at the sky and thought how silly it was. I called Helen from the kitchen floor and told her um I would come. Selling the house took ages, and I cried over every cupboard. I found Alan's pencil tin, his rolled drawings um in the attic, and a dried rose from our wedding. I um gave his old table to a young man, and that felt right. My brother Peter drove over from Harrogate with a van and helped me sort what to keep. We argued over, argued over uh the barometer, which was our father's, and in the end Peter kept it. I took my sewing box, my good knives and a suitcase of photographs. What happened next? The rest went to the shops, and I watched the van go sadly. On the last night I slept on a little bed in the empty room. Next morning the taxi took me to the airport, and Doreen waved from her gate. I never liked flying, so I held a sweet and um looked straight ahead. We landed um in Abu Dhabi at night, and the warm air hit me like an opened oven door. Helen was waiting in arrivals with Sam on her shoulders, her shoulders and Ruby holding um a paper um sign. The sign said welcome Grandma, and the letters were all different colours. My new flat was in Khalidiyah, on the ninth floor, uh with a balcony facing the sea. For a week I could not um sleep, because it was so bright and so quiet. The heat was the um worst thing, and I only went out at dawn. When I first started nursing, there was an old man in the ward who worked with wood. He made me a little bird for my birthday. It was a tiny thing, no bigger than my thumb. I put it on my windowsill at home, and it is still there. Everything smelled different, and it did not rain for ages. Can you tell me more about that? I missed the green terribly, and I stood on the balcony wishing for one um muddy um field. So I bought pots and compost and planted mint, basil and a stubborn little rosemary. The rosemary died twice, and the third one is still alive, and I am very proud of it. My girl took me to the market, and I learned to bargain. A woman in the building brought me sweet things and a hot drink. We could hardly understand each other, but we sat together and laughed at the same things. Within a month I had found uh a choir in a um church hall near the harbour. They were from all sorts of places, and we sang old um songs. I felt like a seedling that had been moved into a bigger pot. The little girl came um to cook with me, and the boy showed um me his work. Some nights I still feel very far from home, especially when it rains. I ring Peter every Sunday, and he tells me about the weather in Yorkshire with great relish, relish. I do not regret the um move, but I do not pretend it was easy. Home turned out to be about the people, more than the place. And my kitchen, with its Yorkshire tea and a little rosemary, is home enough, home enough.
